name: Clouds in Landscape Photos
description: A methods check for every photo-based survey: does the sky in a photo change how much people like the landscape? Tasser, Lavdas & Schirpke (2023, PLOS ONE) took 29 Alpine panoramas shot on sunny summer days and made a second version of each with the clouds removed and the sky recoloured; nothing else was changed. 124 people rated all 58 pictures in a new random order on a 10-point scale (1 = I don't like it at all, 10 = I like it very much), then gave optional background details. Overall, removing clouds made no significant difference when the sky took about 22% of the picture and clouds about 39% of the sky. But more sky raised preference, and a lot of cloud combined with little sky lowered it. Their advice: control the proportion of sky across pictures, not only cloudiness. The template ships with the paper's 58 pictures (S1 Fig, CC BY): alpsNN_clouds.jpg is the original and alpsNN_noclouds.jpg the edited version of pair NN. Analysis as in the paper: a paired t-test per pair (clouds vs no clouds), then a regression of the difference on sky and cloud proportions. Differences from the original study: (1) the survey was in German; the anchors are given in English; (2) the panoramas are the 1000 × 150 pixel versions published in the paper's supplement; the paper does not state the size used in its survey; (3) the background questions follow the paper's list (gender, age group, language, place of residence, school education, field of work), but the answer options are our own; (4) the eye-tracking simulation, photo content analysis and GIS variables the paper used to explain the differences are not part of the template.
